findings.claim: Post item 1 (linkedin-post.txt:11): 'A presigned S3 PUT with a different content-type -> 403'. At HEAD the emulator DOES refuse a query-presigned (X-Amz-*) request whose SIGNED content-type header was changed, but only with --auth on (the default) and only where content-type is in X-Amz-SignedHeaders; with --auth off there is no signature verification at all.
findings.root_cause: There is no separate PutObject content-type check. The framework recomputes the SigV4 signature from the request as received: Signature::of reads SignedHeaders, signature_for re-signs with the actual header values via header_values(parts, name), and a changed signed header yields a different signature -> SIGNATURE_MISMATCH -> ProtocolError::Unauthenticated -> 403. S3 re-words that refusal as SignatureDoesNotMatch with signing diagnostics. PutObject stores the content-type only after the framework admitted the request. If content-type was not signed, changing it does not alter the canonical request (the emulator's own presigner signs only `host` when PresignTarget.headers is empty).

findings.claim: Post lines 7 and 12: 'With auth on, every request needs a SigV4 signature' / 'A request without a valid SigV4 signature -> denied'. At HEAD, --auth on IS the default and routed, sigv4-modeled operations are refused 403 without a valid signature. 'Every request' is too broad: model-derived unsigned operations, unroutable requests, and unsigned public-resource requests behave differently.
findings.root_cause: The CLI default is authentication=true; core/router/src/main.rs:120 installs the process-wide switch; MultiServiceRouter::new registers SigV4Authenticator::for_this_process(); dispatch calls authenticate() only AFTER service selection and operation lookup; authenticate() returns Ok early if no authenticator is registered or the operation's auth_schemes() is an empty slice. Denied is rendered as ProtocolError::Unauthenticated -> 403 by every protocol renderer. The missing-signature code is the emulator's own AccessDenied 'Sign the request with the emulator credentials', not AWS's MissingAuthenticationToken/InvalidClientTokenId.

findings.surface: check-3 / Lambda function URL / resource policy
findings.claim: Post item 3 (line 13): 'A public function URL without lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl -> 403'. At HEAD an ANONYMOUS AuthType=NONE function URL with no resource policy IS refused 403; the check is implemented in the function-URL plane, not by the global SigV4 gate. It is not universal across all function-URL paths.
findings.root_cause: FunctionUrlPlane is mounted three ways (Admits::Anonymous, SignedPublic, SignedRestricted); the anonymous mounting declares auth_schemes Some(&[]) so it bypasses SigV4, but invoked() calls admits_the_caller() for both NONE mountings; invoke_authorization::admits_function_url_request reads the function's resource-based policy at the target qualifier and requires an Allow for INVOKE_FUNCTION_URL_ACTION ('lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl') to the anonymous principal; no policy or a named-principal grant returns Err -> forbidden(403) with AccessDeniedException / {"Message":"Forbidden"}.

findings.claim: Post item 4 (line 14): 'EventBridge -> SQS without a queue policy -> nothing delivered'. At HEAD a direct PutEvents rule with an SQS queue target and no Policy attribute delivers nothing; the refusal is recorded as a failed invocation, dead-letters where the DLQ policy allows, and counts FailedInvocations.
findings.root_cause: PutEvents' queue-target branch calls queue_sends::hand_over, which reads the queue's Policy + KmsMasterKeyId through GetQueueAttributes. queue_delivery_refusal calls state::target_policy_admits, whose whole rule is policy.is_some_and(resource_decision(...) == Allowed): a service principal (events.amazonaws.com) has no identity policies, so no policy = IAM implicit deny. The delivery returns InvocationOutcome::Failed and no Held message is queued, so no SendMessage/SendMessageBatch happens. A customer-managed KMS key on the queue is a second gate (kms:GenerateDataKey).

findings.surface: check-5 / DynamoDB ACTIVE race / 'item 5 was a real bug in our code'
findings.claim: Post items 5 and 17 (lines 15,17): 'A call on a new DynamoDB table before it is ACTIVE -> ResourceInUseException' and 'Number 5 was a real bug in our code. Our emulator hid it for weeks.' At HEAD the emulator DOES model a CREATING window (so it does not hide the race the way Floci did), but the rejection is NOT uniformly ResourceInUseException, the window is a fixed emulator-chosen 3 seconds, and DescribeTable deliberately sleeps through it.
findings.root_cause: STATUS_TRANSITION = 3s; CreateTable stamps active_at = now + 3s; Table::status(now) returns Creating while now < active_at; TableStatus::serves_items() allows only Active|Updating. Control-plane mutations (UpdateTable, DeleteTable, UpdateTimeToLive) on a CREATING table return HTTP 400 ResourceInUseException with 'Table is being created: <name>'; data-plane item operations resolve through active_table/active_table_mut and return item_resource_not_found() ('Requested resource not found'), i.e. ResourceNotFoundException, not ResourceInUseException. DescribeTable computes creation_settles_in(left) and sleeps up to STATUS_TRANSITION before answering, so a waiter never observes CREATING. The 3s span is not configurable (GH #436).

findings.surface: strictness vs over-strictness / auth on, SigV4, resource policies
findings.claim: Post lines 7 and 23: 'it checks more than I said ... With auth on, every request needs a SigV4 signature, and it enforces resource policies' / 'A lenient emulator hides bugs. A strict one that cannot run your code tests nothing.' The strictness is real in code, but the same machinery is measurably OVER-strict: cross-site browser headers, unsigned public reads, and Deny statements over unmodelled condition keys.
findings.root_cause: Three independent mechanisms: (1) refuse_cross_site_browsers() hardcodes RemoteOrigins::SameOriginOnly with allow_remote=false and runs BEFORE authentication for every service; (2) the shared IAM evaluator reads an undecidable condition clause as fail-closed in both directions (collect_applying: 'None if allows => continue', so an undecidable Deny still refuses), and delivery paths that do not publish aws:SecureTransport (DynamoDB and KMS contain zero occurrences of the key in src/; GH #451 names CloudTrail's destination_verdict) therefore let a 'deny non-TLS' statement deny HTTPS requests; (3) the auth gate runs before any resource-policy evaluation, so an unsigned request to a public resource never reaches the policy that would allow it. S3 has a service-specific deny_is_decided() escape hatch and S3/SQS publish the key as true; the EventBridge target_policy_admits and DynamoDB gates call iam::resource_decision directly.
findings.aws_reference: linkedin-post.txt:7,23; GH #451 explicitly diagnoses the root cause: 'Nothing supplies aws:SecureTransport, so the Deny statement's condition stays undecided and is read fail-closed.' GH #438/#26 record AWS serving unsigned public reads and cross-origin presigned requests.

Thus passing the five checks says nothing about whether a given workload's own code can execute.
